title: Changes in latitudes, changes in attitudes
author: Elaine McArdle

dom.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards

st.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition with early-career evidence that high satisfaction can coexist with unequal rewards and workplace disparities. It reports a substantial gender salary gap, racial differences in intentions to leave large firms, and an evidence-based career-counseling response, while appropriately limiting its findings to the cohort’s first years in practice.

For example, at firms with more than 250 lawyers, 67 percent of black attorneys plan to leave within two years, compared to 54 percent of white attorneys.

kp.k: Longitudinal survey establishes an early-career legal profession baseline
kp.d: The article reports initial findings from “After the JD,” not claims about AI. Conducted by David B. Wilkins, the HLS Center on Lawyers and the Professional Services Industry and collaborating organizations, the study tracks nearly 4,000 lawyers over their first 10 career years. Respondents began practice in 2000 and were first surveyed in 2003; further surveys were planned for 2007 and 2011. The sample was 46 percent women and 17 percent nonwhite lawyers, covering 18 regions and nearly every law school, including unaccredited schools. Wilkins cautions that the study raises more questions than it answers.
qs: The study—“After the JD”—is tracking nearly 4,000 lawyers over the first 10 years of their careers.
The respondents, who began practice in 2000, are 46 percent women and 17 percent nonwhite lawyers and are from 18 regions and nearly every law school in the country (including unaccredited schools).
They were first surveyed in 2003 (and their responses were tabulated for the initial report), and they will be questioned again in 2007 and 2011.

kp.k: Early-career job satisfaction challenges assumptions of pervasive unhappiness
kp.d: Nearly three-quarters of the surveyed cohort reported being satisfied or very satisfied with their jobs. Wilkins interprets the findings as showing no evidence of pervasive professional unhappiness, but explicitly limits this conclusion to those who began practicing in 2000; the initial findings concern lawyers two to three years into their careers rather than satisfaction across entire careers.
qs: Lawyers are happier in their careers than is generally believed—in the first few years out of law school, anyway.
According to the study, and contrary to what many believe, there is “no evidence” of “any pervasive unhappiness in the profession,” he says—at least not among those who began practicing in 2000.
To the contrary, in that group, nearly three-quarters reported being “satisfied” or “very satisfied” with their jobs.

kp.k: Work settings offer different rewards and training experiences
kp.d: Wilkins reports that large-firm lawyers were very satisfied with power and prestige but very dissatisfied with their work context, including mentoring and training. Government lawyers reported the opposite trade-off between satisfying work context and public service, and dissatisfaction with compensation. He presents these as distinct combinations of career benefits rather than a single hierarchy of desirable jobs.
qs: “If you look at lawyers in large firms,” says Wilkins, “they are very satisfied with their power and prestige, but very dissatisfied with the context of their work, including the mentoring and training they receive.
Government lawyers are very satisfied with the context and public service aspects of their work, but dissatisfied with the money.
So you can see how different jobs have different mixes of goods.”

kp.k: Compensation varies substantially by practice setting and geography
kp.d: Full-time respondents had a median income of $73,000; about 25 percent reported earning more than $110,000, and the same percentage earned less than $50,000. Large private firms paid the highest salaries, but the article reports substantial geographic variation even there, from $100,000 in Minneapolis to $170,000 in New York City and $172,500 in Connecticut.
qs: The median income of the full-time lawyers surveyed was $73,000, a figure based on a wide range of salaries depending on work setting and geographic location.
About 25 percent of respondents reported making more than $110,000, while the same percentage earned less than $50,000.

Predictably, those in large private firms took home the highest salaries, although the range there was significant—from a low of $100,000 in Minneapolis to highs of $170,000 in New York City and $172,500 in Connecticut.

kp.k: Racial satisfaction differences coexist with unequal departure intentions
kp.d: Wilkins describes racial disparities as less significant than gender disparities in many aspects of the study. More than 80 percent of black attorneys and almost 80 percent of Hispanic attorneys were satisfied with becoming lawyers, compared with about 75 percent of white attorneys. Nevertheless, at firms with more than 250 lawyers, 67 percent of black attorneys planned to leave within two years, compared with 54 percent of white attorneys. These are reported intentions, not observed departures.
qs: Racial disparities were much less significant in many aspects of the study than gender disparities, Wilkins notes.
More than 80 percent of black attorneys and almost 80 percent of Hispanic attorneys report being satisfied with the decision to become lawyers, compared to about 75 percent of whites.
For example, at firms with more than 250 lawyers, 67 percent of black attorneys plan to leave within two years, compared to 54 percent of white attorneys.

kp.k: Women report lower satisfaction despite preferring work substance
kp.d: Wilkins reports significantly lower work-life satisfaction among women than men. Women were happier with the substance of their work but less happy with job setting, including recognition and colleague relationships; social value; and power track, including compensation and advancement opportunities. The findings distinguish substantive engagement from organizational rewards and working conditions.
qs: However, women lawyers reported being significantly less satisfied in their work lives than men did, Wilkins notes

While women are happier than men in the substance of their work, they are much less happy by three other measures: job setting (including recognition received at work and relationships with colleagues), the social value of what they do and power track (including money and opportunity for advancement).

kp.k: Gender pay differences appear within three career years
kp.d: The article reports that women earned less than men in many instances even three years into practice, regardless of work setting. Median salaries were $80,000 for men and $66,000 for women. Researchers planned further study of the gap; the article provides no causal explanation.
qs: One of the most striking findings is that, even three years into their careers, women lawyers were earning less than men in many instances, regardless of the work setting.
The median salary for men was $80,000; for women, it was $66,000.
This gender gap is one aspect that researchers plan to study more carefully.

kp.k: Career education should reflect empirically documented job trade-offs
kp.d: Wilkins proposes using empirical evidence to help students identify their priorities and make informed career choices. The article connects this aim with a new HLS first-year career-counseling program beginning in fall 2006, combining career exploration and summer-job guidance, an assigned counselor for each first-year student's initial appointment, and an orientation led by Wilkins. This is an educational response to the findings, not evidence of improved career outcomes.
qs: While this may seem obvious, Wilkins hopes to use the empirical data to enable law students to make informed choices about careers by recognizing what matters most to them.
“We really are out to try to change the way in which law schools teach about careers,” he says.

The two offices will maintain a unified calendar of programming and events to guide students through career exploration and the practical aspects of looking for summer jobs, and every first-year student will have an assigned career counselor for a first appointment.
